Later generations do not understand this meaning; they merely busily wander about picking up firewood.

A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the 'Single Tune of Yunmen'? Yunmen said, "The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth lunar month. This "Single Tune of Yunmen" penetrates to the very marrow and to the very bone;

the snow has cleared from the thousand peaks, yet they remain cold. The plum blossoms break through their buds, pecking and striking together. The young lord— (Note: The final character "公子" [gōngzǐ] appears to be a scribal error or a fragmentary note, as it does not grammatically conclude the verse. It likely refers to the "Young Master" [gōngzǐ] who is the subject of the poem "Song of the Plum Blossoms" by Li Bai, which is often associated with this kōan.)
The elegant sound of the wooden clapper resounds.
A monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them? Dongshan said, "Why not seek refuge where there is neither cold nor heat?
The monk asked, "What is the place where there is neither cold nor heat? Dongshan said, "Cold."
In winter, cold kills the *ācārya*; in summer, heat kills the *ācārya*.
Cold and heat are clearly explained for you; there is no room for deliberation or to distinguish between the distant and the near. The carrying pole snaps and both ends fall off;
looking up at the vast sky, a new smile arises.
The wind and the banner:
it is neither wind nor banner. Clearly, ten thousand layers of barriers are rent asunder.
Who would have known that, having exhausted all the strength of one’s arms, one would only invite idle fame to fall into the world?
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, "A dried-up shit-stick.
This little sick child of Yunmen lets out a great lion’s roar; he has gained half his nostrils, but he does not realize he has lost his mouth.
Linji asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk gave a shout. Linji gestured for him to sit;
as the monk hesitated, Linji struck him. Another monk came to visit; Linji held up his whisk, and the monk bowed.
Linji struck him. Yet another monk came; Linji held up his whisk, and the monk paid no heed. Linji struck him.
Within a flash of lightning, host and guest are distinguished; upon the back of space, the fundamental principles are established. The livelihood of the Patriarchs was just like this;
later descendants have swept it all away into emptiness.
Zhaozhou says, "Go drink tea. Zhaozhou says, "Go drink tea.
A venomous snake lies across the ancient road; only when you step upon it do you realize it is not what you thought. Even a Buddha is unfit for this task.
It is not mind, not Buddha, and not things. The Master did not know how to read;
Bodhidharma did not understand Chan. In the kingdom of the Great Tang Emperor, the transformation of the three thousand worlds continues as before.
One day the Sixth Patriarch said, "All of you, prepare your boats and oars; I am returning to Xinzhou.
A monk asked, "After the Master has departed, when will he return? The Patriarch replied, "When the leaves fall, they return to the root;
when I come back, I shall have no mouth."
When the clouds part, the sky naturally expands; when the leaves fall, they return to their roots. Turning my head toward the misty waves, I hear the fishermen’s songs passing by the distant village.
A monk asked Zhimen, “What is it like before the lotus has emerged from the water? Zhimen said, “The lotus. He asked again, “What is it like after it has emerged? Zhimen said, “The lotus leaf.”
How is it to emerge from the water compared to not yet emerging? There is a reason for the lotus flower and the lotus leaf. Dīpaṃkara beckoned from afar at the Golden Ground;
the Wise One nodded his head in secret at Jiangling.
A monk asked Muzhou Daowu, "What is the true form of Baizhang? The Master descended from his meditation seat and stood with his hands folded.
The monk asked again, "What is the true form of the Master? The Master ascended the meditation seat once more and sat down.
Baizhang’s cat-face; Guishan’s ghost-eyes. Seeing people, he merely smiles; when handling objects, he does not know their names.
A monk asked Master Tianyi, "How is it before an ancient mirror has been polished? Tianyi said, "It supports the heavens and props up the earth.
The monk asked, "How is it after it has been polished? Tianyi said, "Quickly hide yourself within the shadows of the setting sun."

Supporting the earth and propping up the heavens, his entire being is in action; within the shadows of the setting sun, he does not conceal himself. Sometimes he sits alone on the peak of a solitary mountain;
in profound stillness, one can still hear the frequent sound of falling leaves.
Panshan said: "The moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects have vanished, what is this thing?"

It cannot be described, nor can it be painted. The Sleeping Dragon is forever wary of the clarity of the azure pool. Should one attempt to direct the mind toward its convergence, it remains ultimately beyond comprehension;
the adept must surely be startled in secret.
A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? Lin said, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains.
"In the twelfth month, the mountains burn; heaven is vast, earth is wide; wherever one strikes or bumps into something, it pierces through to the very marrow, making the hair stand on end with cold."
Case: A monk asked the Ancient Tower Master, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Do not! Do not!
He asked again, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Do not! Do not!"
No, no! He draws forth a single broken thread of rope; let the Buddhas and all sentient beings be at liberty—his nostrils, which pierce the heavens, have all been pierced through.
Praise the Buddhas and Patriarchs!

Śākyamuni left the mountains, abandoning the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and casting aside his foolishness; yet at midnight he leaped over the city walls with his heart still unextinguished. He sat in cold meditation for six years without reaching a resolution;
what face does he have to come forth from the mountains?
The forty-eight great vows of Amitāyus Buddha; hundreds of thousands of millions of Amitābhas. The waterfowl and forest trees open the True Eye;
for people, this intimacy requires nothing more.

Avalokiteśvara’s moon is full and round; the stars and constellations are cold. The wind shakes the sea; the thunder splits the mountains. The Great Being of Universal Penetration manifests auspicious responses among humanity.
The Ninth Patriarch.
For half his life his feet did not touch the ground; Xuan knew the roads across the ends of the earth. Having obtained this "pumpkin seal," to this day his eyes stare wide and his mouth hangs agape.
Vimalakīrti.

Deeply entering the gate of non-duality, skillfulness is exhaustively transformed into clumsiness. A single silence settles a thousand differences; he speaks constantly, speaking with blazing intensity.
This clumsy speech endures for ten thousand ages—a pure breeze that pierces through to the very marrow of the bones.
Dharma’s phoenix palace is impenetrable, not even admitting a drop of water. Before the crags of Shaoshi, his discourse was split into two fragments;
he deceived the men and women of others’ households, opening their eyes only to call a tortoise a turtle.
Directly pointing to the Westward Coming is clearly a source of calamity; crossing the river and facing the wall, the thieving mind was not yet extinguished.
From this point on, the skin and marrow were divided and scattered, as a thunderclap resounded through the blue sky.
Crossing the river on a single reed, there is nowhere to bury him. Dividing skin and marrow, he deceives the gods and yells at the ghosts;
in a frantic rush he heads straight west, unaware that he has lost his single sandal.

Master Pang attained the highest degree through the emptiness of mind; his roots were deep and his foundation firm. Together they spoke of non-arising and moved among those of different species, continuing to disturb the Chan school until this very day—unaware that at noon, the third watch is being struck.
Linji’s single blow and single shout overturned mountains and valleys; he utterly disparaged our own school. This thief who steals in broad daylight—this is the Holy One of Jinhua.

A thousand soldiers are not equal to one general; what are such skills compared to the appearance of the command tent? Failing to recognize the Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I prostrate to the Pig-Headed Monk, the Great顛 (Dian) Monk.
Expelling the Head Seat; investigating Sanping’s being struck by an arrow; letting off Han Wen Gong.
A single thread passes through the hook—do not say there are one hundred and eight beads day and night; it is merely like a blind man suing a blind man for being sightless.
The founding ancestor, Master Ying’an, entered the tiger’s den; his grievances were difficult to clear. Throughout the world, Ying’an was known as "the one who holds only a single wedge.
Turning his body within the tiger’s mouth, he squeezed the strange from the very fist. For thirty years he acted recklessly, reviving the orthodox lineage of Dongshan.
Not realizing that one’s transgressions fill the heavens, Master Miam—
whose hands once chewed pigs and dogs—
seeks what "handle" there is to grasp; he raises a fist powerful enough to split open one's chest and blinds one's very crown, thereby bringing forth realization.
He grinds away the blood from one's body and cuts off the life-root of the monk; not a single hair’s breadth will he let pass. To the monastic communities, he is a sworn enemy and a grievous foe.
Such a kind of practitioner will certainly bring misfortune upon his descendants.
At the request of the Elder Zhishan Zhimo, I offer this eulogy for the late Master Mian:
Within the spark struck from flint, he pierced the nostrils of the vast heavens; before the turning of the subtle pivot, he struck the phoenix and snared the dragon.

He extinguished the Eye of the True Dharma within blind donkeys and upheld the orthodox lineage of Linji with his broken sand-pot. His gate and courtyard were steep and precipitous—who would dare to face them?
The Peak: Through an iron wall and silver mountain, a single thread passes through.
Elder Nengren Guangmu requested a eulogy for his portrait;

I, with my blind nature, freely strike out. Using a fist that splits the chest, I sweep away the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials. What does it matter about the "thorny plum" or the "golden circle"?
He has already extinguished the Hu lineage; one knows not what he will leave to his descendants.
Elder Chan Master Shanka of Yunju requests a eulogy for the "human nose" [the essential pivot]. Not a single point exists; even the clear-eyed monk loses his nostrils. An iron mess of food. Gold.
The Iron Circle: Clearly opening the mouth, yet not on the tip of the tongue. This has brought trouble upon later generations, creating deep resentment between Buddhas and patriarchs.
Chan Master Daoyan, the Head Seat, requested a eulogy:
"Self and others are like mountains; fierce temper is like clouds. Cooking rice where there is no grain, he cannot receive those who come. Within a flash of lightning..."
Guest and host are divided; were it not for an old grudge, they would not be neighbors.
Master Zhao, the Head Seat, requests a eulogy for this fellow.
He is too foolish; a single phrase, and even the Buddha does not know it. Old Linji, a hired laborer, [is known throughout] the four heavens.
"Down! Who else is there who dares to open their mouth? A blow across the chest! Head Seat Zhao, do not emulate him; to emulate him is for both parties to fall into a cheap bargain."
The Master cautioned the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable One), requesting his praise:
"Enmity has its source; a debt has its owner. The tortoise-nosed snake, the white-fanged tiger—seizing them alive, captured in the raw, he raises them directly before us."
To trigger the mechanism, one must use a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt.

At the request of Secretary Xilian, I have composed this eulogy for the High Elder Lajiang, whose presence inspires great brilliance. Whether coming from the south or the north, there is nothing with which to meet him: a lacquered bamboo staff.
A casual stroke—watch and see whether the person is present or not. Secretary Lian is truly intolerable; the bright pearl of Zhenhai is suspended in the void and shattered.
Chan Master Dacheng requests a eulogy.

A single scene of sublime splendor—how could it ever be captured by brush and ink? Passed down from patriarch to patriarch, they "follow the error with the error. They do not treat the Buddha-dharma as a matter of worldly sentiment;
before the lightning-fast pivot, they are vividly and unimpededly present.
Attendant Wenwei requested a eulogy:
"Coarse in mind and bold in spirit, with little substance and much falsehood, you blind the eyes of the blind monks and sever the talisman behind the elbow.
The Way of Linji and Dongshan hangs by a thread; moment by moment, you till the soil with the blade and sow with fire, wearing out this decrepit body in the desolate forests and springs."
The mind itself is unique.
At the request of the layman Master Huìwén, I offer this encomium:
Not abiding in seeking the Buddha, not abiding in seeking the Dharma. The eyes and head of devas and humans; the sworn enemy of Buddhas and patriarchs. Pointing downward from below Xiangyan.
South becomes north. Looking up at the tower from the Sword Pond, the tower strikes the tower; the pivot-wheel turns subtly, and not even a single thread can be grasped.
The leviathans refuse to rest. This thief has no face; pointing to the southeast, he looks toward the northwest. He does not stay at Yunju, yet he loathes Jianfu.
Knowing himself unable to maintain the monastic community, he would willingly enter hell for eternal kalpas.
This fellow has been unruly since birth; even Buddhas and Patriarchs find it difficult to approach him. He kicks out the golden ring and the chestnut burr;
his opening of the mouth does not depend on his tongue.

This person is a conduit for the human realm, stubbornly clinging to his ways; unaware that old age has turned him into a demon, he insists on entering the room at every moment, causing much resentment and grievance.
A-he-he! Counting on one's fingers from east to west, who can compare to him? *Du!* (A rebuke).
Three fists under the ribs; a single palm across the cheek. Acting according to the command, who would know the pain or the itch?
A turn of the body and a squeeze to test the fundamental end: Yangqi’s planting of weeds, an iron-hearted liver.
There is not even space enough to set a needle upright; yet there is a jewel of priceless value. Originally, no effort of contrivance is required; when picked up, it fits perfectly.
It is devoid of human sentiment; even the Buddha is swept away. Such a rustic monk lives out his life in empty deception.
Having never traveled to Mount Lu during his peregrinations, he has resided only in Jiang and Zhejiang. He persistently mocks those from all quarters, forgetting his own hundredfold ineptitudes.
Seeking advantage and refuting heterodox views, every thrust and every strike of his is chillingly severe.
A Verse to See Off Chief Librarian Wuzang Returning to Gusu (when Master Xia’an of Lingyin was at Mount Xiwuji): At the side of the Linglong Cliff, a glance—was it seen or not?
He straightens his spine like a bolt of tempered iron. Pointlessly, beneath the forest trees, he errs in his appraisal.
Measuring it out, we take each other’s hands and enter the tiger’s den; suddenly, the turtle is lost within the jar. This matter is perfectly clear—whom shall I tell?
At that time, it was simply this very person; who knew that their eyes would have more dust added to them? I carry my staff and rush north and south;
you enter the western mountains, acting with reckless negligence. You let go of the snake’s head and stroke the tiger’s whiskers; turning around, you—
Acting as one who has stolen his own goods: the vast void is entirely spread before one’s eyes; life and death race together—who dares to peer?
I come with a smile to meet you once more: the nostrils have always hung downward. The family style of Mian is poverty to the bone; Mian has eyes, yet lacks sinews.
Taking the non-existent for the existent—how many can penetrate this "something"? How many can truly penetrate this "something"?
The west wind falls upon the trees as the heavens stretch wide; you, sir, do not remain atop the distant peak.
A single drop from Caoxi is carried on the tip of your staff, swelling the waters of the Wu River by thousands of acres.
Inscription for Director of the Chancellery Zhang’s Yian (Also-an) Hermitage:
Not even a single drop remains at Caoxi; who says the hermitage is named "Also"? I inquire after the Elder Vimalakīrti: an iron wall, and yet another iron wall.
Inscription for the "First Ascent" Meditation Hall:

The Great Way is difficult to align with the myriad things; Even "first ascent" still involves climbing the steps. To turn the body and pass straight through beyond the azure heavens, One must look back to realize that the universe itself is low.
Seeing off Chief Seat Cong for Riyang, also presented to Director Chen (Master Meng’an was at Jingshan at the time):
The first move has no handle; it cuts off all quarters and becomes a taboo. This mind does not turn toward idle white clouds;
with a single staff, he flutters down from the layered emerald peaks. Master Huì’s offenses fill the heavens; the layman, too, is without cause.
How strange! To this day, who knows how many have been deceived? We must all repay our karmic debts from former lives.
When the Venerable Yong of Baiting appeared in the world at Tianxi, I sent him this verse:
"We have followed one another in the forest for years; whether these be good conditions or evil conditions, though we did not receive the transmission on Vulture Peak..."
Record. As for the nostrils, they rest upon that former side.
Meng Zhifu’s heir sought a Dharma name: Xingfu (Arising Blessings). Xingfu is a marvelous child;
blessings are boundless and beyond description. A single point of the numinous terrace—the bright moon in the blue sky.

The arising is dense and subtle, ever-present by your side; all dharmas are likewise so. One stroke achieves two gains; there is no factionalism and no partiality. Among the eight hundred [cases] of Zhaozhou lies the mystery;
this ancestral legacy of the "basket and leather" craft is truly worthy of transmission.
The Magistrate of Mengfu ordered his successor to seek a Dharma name: Xingpu (Rising Gem) and Zhenpu (True Gem).
Without flaw, the ultimate reality is boundless; with an empty mind, one attains the highest degree, bringing glory and radiance to the state and the family.
Xingzhi alone carries on this single lineage. It is preeminent in the human world; its wondrous transformation is continuous and possesses a most distinguished character. Xingzu.

Since the time of the Patriarchs, it has not been possible for generations to accompany [the truth] through mere study. In the daily activities of one who meets the occasion, every single point is fully encompassed.
To Wenbo and Xuanyi, I offer these two verses on bestowing grace:
"When perceiving form with clarity, you see the mind; this mind is neither self nor person. When the moment arrives, do not employ it, but follow along."
Seeking. Whatever is grasped by the hand is fresh in every instance.
The platter rolls the pearl, and the pearl rolls upon the platter. Observe the subtle message within stillness amidst the clamor.
Only when one forgets all intellectual understanding upon the tip of a single hair can one realize that one has been deceived by the eyes all along.

Having fully and exhaustively demonstrated the path of the companion of principle as it is— unmoving like suchness— the road of seeking through phenomena and principle grows ever more remote. Stepping directly beneath and overturning the woodcutter’s path,
I know you have not yet reached Ge Hong’s home.

Inscription for Zhang Sizhi, Director of the Pavilion, titled "The Great Eloquence is Like Stammering; The Great Skill is Like Clumsiness. The vast clarity dots the clouds; a thousand rivers reflect the moon together.
For the sake of my Director of the Pavilion, I have thus spoken these words.
On the "Real Studio" of the Junior Scholar Wang Ziyong:
Regarding the dharmas of this world and worlds beyond, all bases have been overturned; there is only this one reality—view it as pure gold in the fire.

Dwelling in the mountains, the paths are perilous and few people arrive. Living in such poverty, one’s sentiments are called "rustic. The clouds part and the sky is naturally vast; the moon sets as the night deepens into clarity.
The wind stirs a few blades of grass; birds cry out three or four times. Within this, there is boundless meaning—who else is there for me to evaluate it with?
Huìkāngbó requested instruction and was invited to ascend the hall. He raised this case: A scholar named Zhāng Zhuò asked Chángshā [Jiǎoxiu]:
"I have heard the names of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, but I do not know in what lands they dwell. Jiǎoxiu said:
"After Cūihào inscribed upon the Yellow Crane Tower, has any senior gentleman ever inscribed there since? Zhāng Zhuò said: "No. Jiǎoxiu said: "None."
For this topic, one fine passage will suffice. It concerns the verse on Huanghe Lou:
"Taking up a broom to paint the蛾眉 (mei) eyebrows—this is the true message of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
I present it clearly and directly to you."
Seeing off Secretary Liu as he returns to Changle, we meet again and follow one another;
our paths are naturally close. At the summit of the wondrous high peak, I have idly let time pass. Suddenly the karmic winds arise and the waves grow treacherous;
with my single staff, I drift away and arrive in the Seven Min regions.

In the regions of Ou and Min, the Buddha-dharma has been half-extinguished; in the monasteries of Jiang and Zhe, the groves gradually wither. For ten years we have walked hand in hand as if in a single silence;
who would say that life and death belong to different branches?
Far away lies my native land, three thousand li distant; suddenly I recall the moment at my mother’s hall when she saw me off. My staff whistles through the wind as my inspiration knows no bounds;
the heavens of Chu stretch vast and wide, and the distant mountains grow low.
Inscription on the Tomb of Guo Pu at Mount Jinshan:
To truly know the Master’s ground of reality, Behold that azure, towering majesty amidst the waves of Longmen.
If you people of this age would set your eyes upon this side, How could such intimacy compare to arriving there once?
Elder Songguang resides at Xianqin;
those of the same lineage differ from those of different lineages. Every one of them is a water-buffalo of Mount Mui;
once they have become such creatures, when will their pulling of plows and hauling of harrows ever cease?
Seeing off my dharma friend Zen Master Zhelin back to the six regions of Fujian:
ten years of true winter cold. By mountain and by water we lingered together; though pressed down many times, he could not be raised up, yet he never once spoke of the Patriarch’s Barrier.
Mimian’s disciple is his sworn enemy; a fierce flame passing through the wind, the second tally. Within a laugh, there is no point of resolution;
it brooks no lifting up, yet turns all the more elegant.
When a thousand differences are cut off at their source, the path is open; ten thousand miles from home, a single breeze carries the news.
Not failing the personal prediction of Vulture Peak, one waits with earnest hope for the auspicious sound sent by the returning wild goose.
Sending Attendant Xian back to his hometown to visit his kin:
A phrase, no phrase—a wisteria leaning against a tree. Iron walls and silver mountains leave no room for evasion. Three thousand miles away, one’s honored mother;
Upon the tip of a single hair, the whole body is revealed. Muzhou spoke in vain of weaving straw sandals; Xinfeng sells "qiao"—it is not so.
Return! People today are not like those of old; stepping out the door is the very path back home. To Zhìbǐ:
Paying respects at the stupa of Huìnyuán—meeting yet not recognizing one another;
after you have departed, there will only be empty longing. The sacred bones are scattered across the long river; how can the pure breeze ever come to an end?
Within the surging waves of ultimate consciousness, do not seek it elsewhere.
To Master Dingduyuan:

The cauldrons, boiling water, and furnace coals are the bliss of the three dhyānas; the sword-trees and blade-mountains are the site of Great Enlightenment. On this day, clear away the obstructions within the ground of the mind.
Seal. There is not a single Buddha-dharma to be deliberated upon;
the three thousand articles of dharma are for this present age. The perfect luminosity of the one nature must be known by oneself.
Once you have realized the matter of self-knowing, where in the human world will it not shine?
Sizhi transformed the scholars;
drawing his sword from the red dust, he severed the myriad affairs of state. He brought even Buddhas and Patriarchs to their knees like surging waves.
I, for my part, won a hearty laugh; old Sizhen, you are too inconsistent! You should feel ashamed.

At Ge-du Monastery, it is shown that the Buddha-dharma has never been much more than this: benefiting humans and devas beyond the bounds of antiquity. As the staff and the shout fly back and forth, it is difficult to draw near;
one truly knows this to be the ultimate, compassionate heart of the grandmotherly teacher.
Presented to Master Li of Shu:
A single lean staff that has passed through the layered barriers; its traces have vanished from the lakes, rivers, Jiang, and Zhe.
Since attaining the Dharma for settling the mind, Chan, the Way, and the Confucian scholars share this very same school.

The Lady Miàolián requested a general discourse. He raised the following case: A monk asked Fengxue, "When speech and silence involve transcendence and subtlety, how can one pass through them without falling into error?
Fengxue replied, "I always remember that in the third month in Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant.
Thereupon, he spoke this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Where the hundred flowers scent the air, the partridge cries; of a hundred years of light and shade, seventy are rare.
Turning my thoughts back to how many matters there are in this world—losing what was advantageous is itself gaining what is advantageous.

Beating the Dharma drum and seeking verses within inner emptiness, outer emptiness, and both inner and outer emptiness—when a single sound is raised, it is like a sudden clap of thunder. To circulate the Buddha-dharma requires nothing more than this;
for a thousand ages, the majestic atmosphere of Vulture Peak remains sublime.
Venerable Wina Puyan’s lineage at Yezhu is desolate;
the winds and waves of Donghu are most treacherous. How many can truly know his heart?
A solitary falcon in the autumn sky across ten thousand li.
The Venerable Zhengxian roamed Mount Lu, passing through the layered barriers to attain freedom. He vowed to settle scores with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Having no lingering attachment to the scenery of West Lake, he carried Nan Yue and Mount Lu upon the tip of his staff.
The Secretary Yunyi has grown accustomed to returning home;
he has long tasted both licorice and yellow myrobalan. The waves of the great ocean have been tossed up to their very depths.
Having mistakenly swallowed the flavorless water of Cold Spring, he now knows it does not reside upon the tip of the tongue.
Master Lin returns to Shu:
"Clearly, this matter does not depend on another. Eating a meal, one has no reason to bite upon grit. One's own spiritual radiance is utterly lost;
three thousand miles away, one plucks willow blossoms."
Chan Master Chunchun of Sanqu repairs the Buddha Hall;

the Yellow-Faced Gautama lets out a yawn of folly. Employing a thousand schemes and ten thousand stratagems to seek advantage, now that there is no place for him to stand, he must have his descendants cover him over.
The white ox receives guests;

the fields and gardens are secure and peaceful, the white ox at ease. Nearby, it bows to the lake’s radiance; in the distance, it faces the mountains. How could this compare to treading through until not a single inch of soil remains?
The fragrant food of the High Realm lies right within it.
Shi Ru-jing struck the Chan practitioner on the face with three punches, hitting both cheeks. Casting off his hands at the edge of a precipice, he exhausted all his skillful means;
De-yun was not found on some other peak.
The Tea Association requests a verse on:
"The spring breeze blows down the emerald peach blossoms; a single petal flows past a hundred thousand homes. How does this compare to the temple beneath Feilai Peak?
Come, we invite you to drink Zhaozhou’s tea."
Huangbo of Fuzhou sends this to the fundraising master in Guangzhou:
Do not dwell within the first layer of the smoke-basket. To turn the body about, one must examine the ability of those in Lingnan.
It is said that the three thousand disciples on Mount Bo are not equal to the seven hundred monks at Huangmei.

When Huangbo sent out the tea master to engage in the Dharma-battle amidst the hundred grasses, his spear and banners were not yet unfurled, yet his full majesty was revealed. Even if Lu Yu had known the essential point,
he would still have fallen into my second-grade device.
Sending off the Dharma Master of Quanzhou:
A Whistle Without Holes Blown Transversely at Shaolin. Who can truly join in this melody?
On the road by the Luo River in Luoyang at dawn, how many people does a single note awaken?
In the Sangha Hall of Xiangfu Monastery in Quzhou, the transformation-monks lie coiled and dormant like dragons.
A single sheet of idle cloud descends from the azure sky; its unfolding and rolling are inherently free within the immediate occasion.
Let the mosquitoes and gnats do as they please with the wild wind.

To show Layman Wang: when you study Chan and awaken to the Way, you become stained by mud and sand. Seeing the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like giving birth to an enemy. Breaking through the dust and hitting the mark, you plant thorns;
standing ten thousand fathoms high, there is still error. This is a great mistake! This is a great mistake! Cut it in two with one stroke—amidst the flames...
The lotus flower has no skill at all; its livelihood is found everywhere.

Disciple Nan, returning to Puyang—if you take these words as the fixed framework of the school, then even the Vulture Peak would be insufficient, and the entire earth, though gathered together, would yield not a single grain of millet.
A single grain. It makes me reminisce about Old Master Zenglang.
Attendant Ziz begged for alms;
he did not study literature nor did he study calligraphy. He was diligent in the Way, forgetting his own body as he pushed through the mounds of yellow dust.
It turns; let it be carried away at will by the pure wind into the great void.
Moreover, when the attendant held his bowl at Vulture Peak, there was no dharma to transmit to others. The Linji school’s style has been utterly extinguished; only the true man of the Way knows this.
My mind! With a sincere heart, I lift up the broken sand-basin.

When receiving guests with tea and food, there is nothing in the household to offer as accompaniment. In responding to the moment, one never relies on premeditated arrangement. When a guest comes to the gate—
A visitor asked, "Where have you come from this morning?

Chan Master Chao replied, "Holding my almsbowl amidst the whistling autumn winds, I travel at ease, following my inspiration. As I walk, I swing my arms; from the southern regions to the northern lands, I buy hats to fit my heads."

They have already attained the highest degree at Vulture Peak.
With ten billion emanated bodies, he benefits sentient beings; the donkey’s jaw and the horse’s chin are indeed difficult to discern. Sometimes, amidst the clamor, he casually extends a hand;
the intent lies in the hook-tip, not in the star.
Daily activities are clear and distinct, straight as a string; do not defile the field of the mind with the Buddha-dharma. He himself says there are no immortals in the world;
even the aged Vimalakīrti has only attained half.

Without relying on one's own lot, one insists on practicing Chan; selling off the ancestral fields before the mountain, he sets out empty-handed with no means of livelihood—truly, a fine son never spends his father’s money.

Master Yuan holds aloft his torch: when he stays, he stays; when he walks, he walks. With every step he takes outside the gate, a pure breeze arises. Cold? Not cold. Heat? Not heat. Intense!
A flake of snow flying amidst a mass of flames; coming thus from ten thousand miles away. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, there is neither birth nor death.
Since there is neither birth nor death, tell me, where has Elder Yuan gone? Depart! Depart! The great ocean dries up and empty space shatters.

Written by Lu You, Grand Master of the Palace (Taizhong Dafu), Attendant at the Baomu Pavilion (Baomuge Dazhi), and retired from service.
Chan Master Songyuan’s name was Chongyue. He was born into the Wu family of Songyuan in Longquan County, Chuzhou;
thus, he took this as his own style name. From childhood, he was outstanding and extraordinary; even among a crowd of children, he never engaged in frivolous play. As he grew slightly older...
Chang heard of the supramundane Dharma and yearned for it. At twenty-three, he left home and donned the robes of a temple-sweeper.
He received the five precepts at Daming Temple and first visited Master Lingshi Miaochan. Subsequently, he went to Mount Jing to see Master Dahui Zonggaop.
After some time, Dahui ascended the hall and remarked that Master Hua of Jiangshan was a man of direct and swift capacity. Upon hearing this, the Master...

He waited for dawn before departing. Upon his arrival, he entered the room, but before he could reach a point of realization, he withdrew. He redoubled his efforts and spent the entire night contemplating the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
Suddenly, he attained enlightenment and went immediately to consult Ying’an. When Ying’an cited the words, “The World-Honored One has a secret word;
Kāśyapa did not conceal it,” the Master replied, “This leaves the Master at a loss. Ying’an let out a piercing shout. From that time on—

He consulted with Ying’an morning and evening, who was greatly pleased and regarded him as a vessel of the Dharma. He spoke a verse encouraging him to shave his head so that he might become a pillar of our Way.
In the second year of the Longxing era, the Master received full ordination at the White Lotus Hermitage on West Lake in Lin’an.

From then on, he traveled extensively to the gates of the great masters throughout Jiang and Zhe, yet rarely found one whose mind accorded with his own. Thereupon, he crossed the sea and entered Min, where he went to see Qian.
One day, Zen Master Genkuan Eiryū took his leave of Mukan. Mukan cited the saying: "A phrase, no phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree.
The Master said, "Torn asunder! Mukan said, "Layuan said, 'What a pile of rotten firewood! What do you say to that? The Master said, [silently].
"Adding a point to an arrowhead. Thus he engaged in such exchanges several times. Mokuan said, "My elder brother’s responses are such that even an old monk like I cannot surpass them;
yet, they are still not it. In the future, when the fly-whisk handle is in your hands, you will be unable to act for others, nor will you be able to test others."
The Master said: "To lead others—to cause an ordinary person of common ground to transcend directly into the realm of the sages—is indeed difficult.
But to examine a person—striking them as they pass before one's eyes, knowing their very marrow before they have even opened their mouths—what difficulty is there in that?
Mudan raised his hand and said: "I have told you clearly: when the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue; you should know this for yourself."
More than a year later, he met Mian Hua at Xishan in Quzhou. Whenever Mian asked him something, he would answer immediately. Mian smiled and said, "Huangyang Chan;

you are truly one who is so intent on clarifying the Way that you have even forgotten to sleep or eat. When Mian moved to Jiangshan, Huazang, and later Jingshan, the Master followed him to all these places.
Once, during a session in Mian’s inner quarters, Mian asked a monk standing nearby, "It is not a Buddha, nor is it an object. The Master [stepped forward].
Serving by his side, he attained sudden and great enlightenment, whereupon he said: "Today I have finally understood Master Mukan’s way: 'The opening of the mouth does not depend on the tongue.
From then on, his eloquence and discernment were unrestrained and his sharp edge was unassailable. When Miyuan moved to Lingyin, he appointed the Master as the First Seat.
Subsequently, the Master entered the world at Chengzhao in Pingjiang as a successor to Miyuan, and later moved to Jiangyin.
Guangxiao in Wuchang, Wuweizhi in Yuzhou, Jianfu in Raoyang, Xiangshan in Mingzhou, and Huqiu in Pingjiang are all famous mountains throughout the realm;
yet among them, Wuweizhi is the most secluded and was further devastated by fire. When the Master arrived there, he took up residence.
Patch-robed monks arrived from the four quarters, and the monastic buildings flourished once more. People said that the Master could cause even a mountain to become large.

In the third year of the Qingyuan era, the seat at Lingyin was vacant; everyone asked, "How can we obtain Master Yue? It so happened that he was granted the appointment by imperial decree, and the sound of joy rose like the tide.
He resided there for six years; his Way flourished, those who attained the Dharma were numerous, and his position became preeminent.
At that time, Master Guan harbored the aspiration to retire from public life; he immediately submitted a petition to the Emperor requesting to be relieved of his duties as abbot.

The Emperor, perceiving his sincerity, granted his request. He retired to the Eastern Hermitage, where he soon suffered from a slight illness, yet he did not neglect his propagation of the Way even in his infirmity.
Suddenly, he personally wrote a letter bidding farewell to the various officials and nobles, and further provided two statements to test his students, saying:
"Why is it that a person of power cannot lift their foot? When the mouth opens, it is not on the tongue.

He also sent a letter to Xiangshan Guangmu and Yunju Shanka, who had succeeded him in the Dharma, entrusting them with the Great Dharma. Thereupon, he wrote a verse, which began: "Coming, there is no place..."
He arrived; he departed, yet there was nowhere to which he went. In a sudden, pivotal turn at the profound gate, even Buddhas and patriarchs were at a loss.
He sat in *paryaṅka* and entered stillness on the fourth day of the eighth month in the second year of the Jiading era. He had reached the age of seventy-one and had spent forty summers in retreat.
His entire remains were enshrined in a stupa on the slopes of North Peak. Four years after the completion of that stupa, Xiangshan sent his attendant Daofu [with this message].

Having passed the age of eighty and lying ill upon a single bed, he did not even notice that he rose to his feet upon receiving the letter and said:
"My deceased friend Linchuan Li De-yuan—Hao indeed heard the Way from Ying’an, for he was a fellow student with Mi’an. De-yuan used to speak with me often."
The occasions and dialogues concerning his inquiries and moments of awakening generally continued until dawn.

Now, reading the Master’s words, they are steep and towering, looking down upon clouds and rain like Mount Hua at five thousand *zhang*; they kick against the heavens and ride upon the void, startling the heart and dazzling the eyes.
It was like the tide at Haimen on the Qiantang River, where tigers and leopards trembled with fear and roof tiles shook and fell; it was like the battle of Kunyang during the Han dynasty.
Only by reflecting upon what Deyuan had said can one then know that the Master was a true descendant of Linji’s orthodox lineage and of Ying’an and Mi’an. The inscription says:
The single school of Linji is the authentic transmission of the Buddhas of the past. Master Ying’an and his disciples swallowed the golden circle and the chestnut burr with a single mouth;
later, they transmitted it to Songyuan. At Songyuan’s initial resolve, he practiced Chan for kalpas within a single laugh.
Like a swift thunderclap shattering a mountain, he presided over eight monastic seats, where the assembly was like surging waves.
The golden-tipped arrow leaves the hand, shattering bones and rending the liver; what does that deluded one know?
Ten great kalpas after the iron gates of ten thousand li, when mountains are crushed and rivers submerged, this stupa remains towering and firm, sustained by the power of the Dharma.

Yet, regarding the essential meaning of Shaolin and the authentic transmission of Dongshan, it would have been impossible to manifest the greatness of that time without this record.

The stream of Caoxi flowed eastward into the Land of the Rising Sun in more than twenty branches.
Of those, ten originated from Songyuan, and the lineage of Tianze was particularly prolific in extending the flow of Songyuan, permeating our country to such an extent. And so it was.

It has been a long time. Yet its two-volume *yulu* (recorded sayings), the old edition having perished, is now on the verge of becoming as non-existent as the "son of the copyist" (a metaphor for something lost).
In recent times, even the dilapidated and worn-out texts are frequently destroyed by fire; this is still not avoiding the fate of the Qin dynasty, which lacked the character for "fire.
How can those under the imperial canopy remain complacently indifferent to such a lapse in the canonical record?
